content: People from minority groups who have asthma often experience worse health outcomes compared to the general population. These outcomes include more frequent visits to doctors for acute asthma flare-ups. Various educational programs designed to empower individuals with asthma have been shown to improve specific outcomes, such as better adherence to treatment, increased asthma knowledge among children and their parents, and improved cost-effectiveness of care. Chronic disease management models for minority groups often emphasize the cultural context of the individual, rather than focusing solely on the disease symptoms. This raises the question of whether asthma education programs tailored to specific cultural needs are effective in improving asthma-related outcomes, feasible to implement, and cost-effective. The objective of this review was to determine whether culture-specific asthma education programs, compared to generic asthma education programs or usual care, improve asthma-related outcomes in children and adults from minority groups. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, and Embase. The search also included review articles and reference lists of relevant studies, with the most recent search completed in June 2016. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared culture-specific asthma education programs with generic programs or usual care in adults or children from minority groups with asthma. Two independent reviewers selected, extracted, and assessed the data for inclusion. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. In this updated review, three additional studies involving 220 participants were included, bringing the total to seven RCTs. These studies involved 837 participants, ranging in age from 1 to 63 years, all from ethnic minority groups. The methodological quality of the studies was rated as very low to low. For the primary outcome—asthma exacerbations during follow-up—the quality of evidence was low across all outcomes. In adults, culture-specific programs did not significantly reduce the number of participants experiencing one or more exacerbations during follow-up (odds ratio [OR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.50 to 1.26), hospitalizations over 12 months (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.31 to 2.22), or exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.73). However, culture-specific programs did improve asthma-related quality of life (QoL) scores in 280 adults from two studies (mean difference [MD] 0.26, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.36). It is important to note that this improvement in QoL was less than the minimal important difference for the score. In children, culture-specific programs were more effective than generic programs or usual care in reducing severe asthma exacerbations requiring hospitalization, as shown in two studies involving 305 children (rate ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.95). These programs also improved asthma control in one study with 62 children and QoL in three studies with 213 children. However, culture-specific programs did not significantly reduce the number of exacerbations during follow-up (OR 1.55, 95% CI 0.66 to 3.66) or the number of exacerbations overall (MD 0.18, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.62) in 100 children from two studies. The authors concluded that the available evidence suggests culture-specific education programs for adults and children from minority groups are likely effective in improving certain asthma-related outcomes. However, the review was limited by the small number of studies and the very low to low quality of evidence. Not all asthma-related outcomes improved with culture-specific programs for both adults and children. Despite these limitations, the findings suggest that culture-specific asthma education programs may be beneficial, particularly for children. These programs are often more time-intensive, but their potential benefits warrant further investigation. More robust RCTs are needed to strengthen the quality of evidence and to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of culture-specific programs.
